records.title: Extreme Heat and Family Fertility Decisions: Evidence From Rural China
records.abstract: ABSTRACT This paper examines how extreme heat affects fertility behavior among rural households in China. Using nationally representative survey data from the 2010–2015 waves of the CGSS, we show that greater exposure to harmful degree days (HDD) during the growing season significantly reduces households' fertility intentions—measured by the ideal number of children—and also lowers actual fertility. The evidence suggests that extreme heat depresses agricultural income and raises child‐rearing costs, consistent with a quantity–quality trade‐off. We further find that extreme heat weakens son preference. Importantly, adaptation measures such as agricultural insurance and crop diversification help buffer these adverse effects. These findings highlight the need for climate‐adaptation policies to mitigate the impact of extreme heat on demographic behavior in developing regions.

records.title: IoT-Based Smart Soil Regeneration Tracking System Using ESP32 with AI-Based Soil Nutrient Prediction, Future Crop Recommendation & Automated Soil Rejuvenation Control
records.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
records.abstract: Soil health plays a critical role in agricultural productivity, environmental sustainability, and crop quality. This paper presents an IoT-based smart soil regeneration tracking system using ESP32 with AI-based soil nutrient prediction, future crop recommendation, and automated soil rejuvenation control. The proposed system integrates soil moisture, TDS, and DHT11 sensors to continuously monitor soil and environmental parameters in real time. Sensor data is transmitted through IoT technology to the Blynk platform and Flask application for remote monitoring and analysis. Random Forest and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) algorithms are utilized for soil nutrient prediction, crop recommendation, and future soil condition forecasting. Based on analytical results, the system automatically controls irrigation pumps and valves to maintain suitable soil conditions. The developed system improves water management, reduces manual monitoring, enhances soil fertility assessment, and supports sustainable smart farming practices with efficient resource utilization and accurate decision-making. The architecture provides reliable real-time monitoring capabilities and enables intelligent agricultural automation for improving long-term soil productivity efficiently.

records.title: The effect of maternal employment during preschool years on school readiness
records.abstract: Many children referred because of “learning disability” have mothers in full‐time employment. This study was undertaken to examine the effect of maternal employment on school readiness. One hundred and seven children were studied. Forty‐six were the offspring of women who had not gone out to work since the birth of the child (group A). The mothers of the other 61 had worked for 1 year or more during the lifetime of the child (group B). The mother of each child completed a detailed questionnaire. Each child was subjected to standardized tests of reasoning, numerical ability, Gestalt, verbal comprehension, eye‐hand co‐ordination, visual and auditory perception and IQ. Groups A and B were compared with regard to marital status of parents, their educational attainments, family size, ordinal position of the index child and years of nursery school experience. Educational attainments of both fathers and mothers were significantly higher in group A and children had spent significantly longer at nursery school. Group B (working mothers) had a predictably higher incidence of single parents. Comparison of results showed no significant difference between groups A and B for 6 of the 8 tests administered. Group B results did not differ significantly when divided into categories according to years of maternal employment. The study suggests that there is no direct relationship between maternal employment and maturity at school entry.

records.title: Differential fertility and contraceptive prevalence rate in Korea
records.abstract: Koreas total fertility rate declined by 65% in the 1960-85 period from 6.0 to 2.1. National fertility surveys indicate strong differentials on the basis of factors such as age region education age at 1st marriage sex preference for child and female employment status. Although fertility has generally been lower among women with higher levels of educational attainment this differential was reduced in the 1974-85 period especially among women 30-39 years of age. The impact of urban versus rural residence on fertility has also been significantly reduced since the early 1960s when Koreas national family planning program was implemented. The gap in average number of children ever born between urban and rural women is narrowest among younger women. Mean age at 1st marriage has risen in Korea from 21.6 years in 1960 to 24.1 years in 1980. Again the gap in number of children ever born by age at marriage has declined since 1974. Son preference continues to exert an upward trend on family size. Finally several surveys indicate that women who worked before marriage have significantly lower fertility levels than women who were not so employed; however there seem to be no significant fertility differential between current female workers and nonworkers.

records.title: The social policy of Belarus and the development of human potential: Problems and solutions
records.abstract: The article is devoted to the analysis of the directions and mechanisms of adapting the social policy of Belarus to the demographic, migration, communication and technological challenges of modern society. The purpose of the article is to search for social policy mechanisms aimed at developing human potential and stimulating the social activity of citizens. The author analyses the directions of the state’s social policy in the absence of the reproduction of labor resources, an increase in the demographic burden on the ablebodied population, an uneven distribution of labor resources, the emigration of skilled personnel, growth in automation and robotization of production, and a growing need to build effective communication between the government and the population. The article provides an extensive analysis of statistical information, sociological research data, the legislative framework, methods and social technologies of social policy. As a result of the study the author comes to the conclusion that it is necessary to search for new mechanisms for implementing social policy in various fields. Therefore, in the field of demography, it is advisable to search for indirect measures to increase social guarantees for women in order to stimulate fertility, and transform the pension system in order to reduce the demographic burden on the working population. In the field of migration, it is advisable to take government action to prevent the outflow of highly qualified specialists abroad and to return of students who have received education abroad. In the field of social and labor relations existing personnel technologists should be improved and objective methods for evaluating the effectiveness of employees based on a competency-based approach should be introduced. In the field of communication between society and the state it is necessary to inform the public about the current state policy and to organize public discussions of the state initiatives before making them.

records.title: Advances in Stem Cell Biology – an ASGBI International Conference held at Durham University
records.abstract: During the past decade, the field of stem cell biology has received increasing amounts of attention from scientists, ethicists, industrialists, politicians and the general public. This recent interest was primarily stimulated by the derivation of human embryonic stem cells in the late 1990s (Thomson, 1998) and the recognition that such cell lines could be used as a potential renewable source of human tissue for therapeutic applications. It is sometimes difficult to encapsulate the speed at which developments in this field have occurred during the last 10 years. These changes are on a global scale and range from debate and creation of government policy, establishment of international centres of excellence in stem cell science, huge levels of investment both in the public and the private sector, and massive recruitment of scientific expertise and training directed toward stem cell science. It must be acknowledged, however, that ‘stem cell science’ as we know it today has a long history and encompasses work by researchers over many decades from multiple disciplines including embryologists, basic cell biologists investigating processes in both health and disease, and biologists studying developmental systems. Stem cell science appears to be evolving as a discipline in its own right, drawing on many of these and other core subjects. Indeed, this multi-disciplinary approach is set to expand as the sciences of stem cells and regenerative medicine come together and new translational approaches for the clinic are developed. This process will require the input of other technologies from traditionally non-biological subjects such as chemistry, physics and engineering, to create new applications and solutions to existing problems by drawing on a broad base of knowledge. To provide a snapshot of some of the recent advances in stem cell science and a flavour of the breadth of this growing discipline, an international symposium entitled ‘Advances in Stem Cell Biology’ was held at Durham University, UK, during July 2007. The symposium was divided into several discrete themed sessions each introduced by leaders in their field. The subject matter extended from basic cell biology of stem cells and the molecular mechanisms that control their self-renewal and commitment to differentiation, through to using stem cells to engineer specific tissue types. This Summer Meeting of the Anatomical Society of Great Britain and Ireland (ASGBI) (http://www.anatsoc.org.uk/) was held in association with the Northeast England Stem Cell Institute (NESCI) (http://www.nesci.ac.uk/). The symposium began with a themed session on nuclear transfer and reprogramming. Sir John Gurdon (Cambridge, UK) started proceedings by giving an outline of his pioneering research from the 1950s demonstrating the concept of nuclear transfer. His presentation focused on the background and present state of research in the derivation of embryo cells by nuclear transfer. He described how the differentiated state of adult somatic cells is very stable. It is very rare for cells committed to one pathway of differentiation to change direction and enter a different specialization pathway. However, if the nucleus of such a determined or differentiated cell is transplanted into an egg or oocyte of an amphibian or mammal, a dramatic nuclear reprogramming event can take place. Accordingly, cells with characteristics of those found in the embryo can be derived from the nuclei of somatic cells and show the expression of known molecular markers of stem cells. However, in some instances, somatic cell nuclei retain a memory of their original pattern of gene expression prior to nuclear transfer, even when they have been grown through several generations. Sir John outlined our current understanding of the mechanisms by which somatic cell nuclei are reprogrammed to a rejuvenated pattern of gene expression. The changes that are induced by egg or oocyte cytoplasm fall broadly into three classes: (1) the removal of marks that characterize the differentiated state of the nucleus. These include the demethylation of genomic DNA in the promoter region of genes that undergo reprogramming and the removal of modified proteins associated with inactive state of genes; (2) the provision by host cells of those transcription factors required to transcribe genes that undergo activation; (3) the decondensation of chromatin to provide access to transcription factors to the regulatory regions of activated genes. It was noted that experiments performed on Xenopus eggs and mammalian oocytes facilitated the identification of the molecules and mechanisms involved by virtue of their large size and abundant material. In 2006, Sir John published a personal historical account of events leading from the earliest success in vertebrate nuclear transfer to the current hope that nuclear reprogramming may facilitate cell replacement therapy (Gurdon, 2006). Nuclear reprogramming and the epigenetic control of stem cells was a subject considered by the next speaker in this session, Lyle Armstrong (Newcastle, UK). He gave an overview of the importance of Hox gene clusters and their activation during the early stages of embryogenesis to determine the pattern of the body axis. However, the expression of Hox genes is understood to be repressed in pluripotent stem cells and is activated during onset of differentiation. The subject of whether the differentiation of embryonic stem cells establishes the correct Hox code and whether Hox clusters were subject to epigenetic control in embryonic stem cells was discussed. Some of the material presented has recently been published (Atkinson et al. 2008). In a subsequent presentation, Chris Hutchison (Durham, UK) described how the architecture of the nucleus, in particular that of the nuclear envelope, was understood to play an important role in the regulation of adult stem cell function. In a paper by Pekovic and Hutchison featured in this issue, the authors examine the maintenance of the stem cell niche in the context of ageing and introduce the role of lamins, a family of nuclear envelope proteins, as intrinsic modulators of ageing in adult stem cells. The second themed session focused on stem cell self-renewal and potency. In the brain, Wieland Huttner (Max Planck, Dresden Germany) described the mechanism of cell proliferation and differentiation within the murine neuroepithelium. During neurogenesis, neuroepithelial cells undergoing cell proliferation exit the cell cycle and express the anti-proliferative gene Tis21. It was shown how the expression of Tis21 linked to GFP could be used as a tool to distinguish between proliferating and differentiating neuroepithelial cells and revealed the existence of a novel neuroprogenitor population. During his presentation, Professor Huttner went on to describe his work concerning the symmetric versus asymmetric distribution of the apical plasma membrane [as defined by the expression of membrane protein, Prominin-1 (CD133)] during proliferative versus neuron-generating divisions of neuroepithelial cells (Götz & Huttner, 2005). Germline stem cells, which can self-renew and generate gametes, are unique stem cells in that they are solely dedicated to transmit genetic information from generation to generation. During his presentation, Karim Nayernia (Newcastle, UK) spoke about his work on adult male germline stem cells (spermatogonial stem cells) and their conversion into embryonic stem-like cells which possess the developmental potential to form cells of all three germ layers. As explained in his review article herein, understanding how spermatogonial stem cells can develop into pluripotent stem cells and how somatic stem cells can give rise to germ cells could provide significant insight into the regulation of developmental totipotency as well as having important implications for male fertility and regenerative medicine. Several reports have shown that the cell cycle of self-renewing embryonic stem cells is different to that of normal somatic stem cells. These unusual features were reviewed by Majlinda Lako (Newcastle, UK) during her presentation on cell cycle regulation in human embryonic stem cells. The cell cycle of embryonic stem cells is characterized by a larger S phase and truncated G1 phase. It is recognized that the transition between these phases is highly regulated by the expression and phosphorylation of several well-known cyclins, cyclin-dependent kinases and members of the retinoblastoma gene family. The role of these components in the regulation of G1 to S phase transition in somatic and embryonic stem cells is reviewed in this issue, in relation to the maintenance of stem cell pluripotency. The first of two themed sessions focusing on epithelial stem cells was opened by Fiona Watt (Cambridge, UK) who discussed stem cells and lineage selection in the mammalian epidermis. The skin, particularly the epidermis, is a valuable system to study the properties of adult stem cells. Mass transcriptional profiling has revealed several new markers and regulators of the stem cell compartment. Elucidation of the mechanisms by which stem cells are maintained and commit toward restricted modes of differentiation have revealed the involvement of specific signalling pathways that control lineage specification as cells exit the stem cell compartment (Watt et al. 2006). Furthermore, pertubation of such signalling can contribute toward the development of keratinocyte tumours. Continuing with the subject of epidermal stem cells, Ian Mackenzie (London, UK) presented his work on stem cell renewal in both health and disease states. The topic of cancer stem cells was introduced whereby a solid tumour resulted from a distinct population of malignant stem cells. These ‘tumour-initiating’ cells may be distinguished from healthy stem cells by various means. Emphasis was drawn toward the value of in vitro models in which persistence of stem cell patterns may provide insight into the properties of malignant stem cells (Mackenzie, 2006). The review appearing in this issue covers some of the latest work in the field of epithelial stem cells and malignancy. The topic of stem cells in the skin was concluded by a presentation given by Colin Jahoda (Durham, UK), who discussed the stem cell features of the hair follicle and their developmental potential and role in wound healing and regeneration. It is well established that the follicle dermis has inductive properties and can reprogram epithelia into skin and follicles and may play a role in skin repair. However, more recently, the same cells have revealed a much broader stem cell potential (Waters et al. 2007). The second themed session on epithelial stem cells was led by David Breault (Harvard, USA), who discussed his work on stem cells within the epithelium of the small intestine. Through the creation of telomerase (mTert)-GFP transgenic mice, a new system has been created to identify stem cells in adult tissues. This model was used to identify, isolate and purify stem cells from the intestinal crypt, which were subsequently functionally characterized as being able to give rise to absorptive and secretory lineages. Moreover, such cells specifically engraft the intestinal stem cell niche during fetal development and persisted long term in adult chimeric animals. A review article featured in this issue highlights the need to produce model systems such as the Tert-GFP mouse to identify and isolate intestinal stem cells that can be functionally assessed. The subject of gut stem cells was continued by Naomi Willis (Durham, UK), who gave a thorough review of the mechanisms understood to regulate stem cell turnover and differentiation in the normal large intestine. Identification of the colonic stem cell niche has been hampered by the absence of reliable markers. Perturbations in stem cell dynamics are generally believed to represent a first step towards the formation of colorectal tumours. Accordingly, there is demand to identify new reliable markers of the stem cell niche in the large intestine that will be of value to basic research and the development of diagnostic and prognostic tools for use in colorectal cancer. This topic is further explored in an article featured in this issue, where progress in searching for putative markers of colonic and colorectal stem cells is reviewed. Switching attention to haematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) in the fifth session, Len Zon (Harvard, USA) commenced proceedings by giving an initial overview of the derivation of HSCs during embryonic development and in the adult. The zebrafish was shown to be a very effective model to study HSC regulation and has contributed greatly to embryonic haematopoiesis (de Jong & Zon, 2007). Many mutations and specific chemicals have been found to affect the production of HSCs as a consequence of studying such models. For example, prostaglandin E2 is a potent activator of blood stem cells as well as adult homeostasis (North et al. 2007). Tariq Enver (Oxford, UK) followed with a presentation on the molecular regulation of normal and leukaemic stem cells. The value of obtaining a definitive collection of specific biomarkers was highlighted for phenotypic identification of stem cells and cancer stem cell surveillance. Anne-Marie Buckle (Manchester, UK) described how HSCs represent one of the best characterized stem cell systems to date, and which has successfully been used in the clinic as part of bone marrow transplant therapy for many years. A key goal, however, is the need to develop systems which enable the ex-vivo expansion of blood cells, which is dependent upon understanding the signalling mechanisms that regulate stem cell self-renewal and differentiation. To close the theme on blood stem cells, Antony Green (Cambridge, UK) spoke about the evolution of a blood stem cell enhancer of the SCL gene, which has a key role in haematopoietic development (Ogilvy et al. 2007). The final session of the symposium considered the application and use of stem cells in tissue engineering and translation into the clinic. Chris Mason (London, UK) started the session and gave a broad overview of the requirements for translational research, including the need for consistency of materials, understanding of bioprocessing, scale-up procedures, reproducible procedures and cost effectiveness. Some of these issues are highlighted practically in a recently published article on the culture of embryonic stem cells (Veraitch et al. 2008). He demonstrated how automation and the recruitment of robots could be employed to address some of these issues, such as the reproducible expansion of cultured human embryonic stem cells. Paul Sharpe (London, UK) described how teeth develop as a result of the interaction between epithelia and mesenchyme and showed how this process could be replicated in the laboratory. Understanding of these early developmental processes has enabled the development of methods to produce human tooth primordia from cultured stem cells for transplantation into the adult mouth (Yen & Sharpe, 2008). Stem cells from embryonic and adult sources have proven useful for such applications. In the final presentation of this session, Kevin Shakesheff (Nottingham, UK) showed how tissue engineering scaffolds are designed to influence the physical environment surrounding a cell population. Environmental cues can be divided into surface effects, soluble molecules, biomechanical forces and population effects. Management of these factors was demonstrated through the design of specialized materials, including injectable scaffolds with co-delivery of cells and extracellular matrix for tissue reconstruction in vivo. These and other issues concerning the custom design of scaffolds and sources of stem cells suitable for such tissue engineering applications are further discussed in a review article featured in this issue. The symposium drew to a close with an overview of the newly formed UK National Stem Cell Network (UKNSCN; http://www.uknscn.org) by Ben Sykes (BBSRC, UK). Further details about the UKNSCN can be found in this issue. Overall, the symposium was an outstanding success and was very well attended. The event provided an excellent forum for the discussion of recent developments in the stem cell arena. The high standard of work presented by the contributors stimulated much interaction and was thought-provoking. The organizers would like to thank each of the speakers for their contributions and all those involved in helping to organize and administer the operation of this event and the publication of this special symposium issue of the journal.

records.title: The Limits of Nominal Problem-Solving Why Global Problems Remain Unresolved and Reproduced: Toward a UPCT Theory of Generative-Resonant Civilization
records.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
records.abstract: Central Claim in One Sentence Global problems remain unresolved because modern civilization reduces dynamic relational crises to static nominal problems and attempts to control them as (S), whereas UPCT reframes problems as closures or ruptures of (ΦR) and evaluates solutions by whether they reopen generative resonance over time. Description Modern civilization has not ignored global problems. It has built institutions, policies, indicators, expert committees, international agreements, ethical frameworks, governance systems, and technological interventions to address climate change, declining birthrates, war, food insecurity, inequality, discrimination, and AI ethics. Yet these problems persist, mutate, and often reappear through the very systems designed to solve them. This paper argues that the deepest reason lies in the ontology of modern problem-solving. Modern civilization tends to transform dynamic relational processes into static nominal problems: climate change becomes CO2, demographic decline becomes fertility rates, war becomes security, food insecurity becomes production volume, inequality becomes redistribution, discrimination becomes attribute management, and AI ethics becomes transparency, fairness, accountability, and safety. These reductions are partially valid and practically necessary, but they obscure the wider fields of relation from which the problems emerge. Drawing on the Universal Phase Crystallization Theory, or UPCT, the paper identifies this pattern as nominal problem-solving. Under the implicit ontology (E = S), existence is treated as structure, classification, measurability, manageability, and fixed meaning. Problems are stabilized as (S), and solutions are pursued through further (S): institutions, targets, regulations, audits, indicators, standards, and governance frameworks. This often generates the spiral (S → S' → S'' → Hyper-S), in which problem-solving becomes structural self-reproduction. Against this, the paper proposes (E = ΦR): existence as generative possibility and relational resonance. A problem is not simply a named object, but the closure, rupture, or over-crystallization of (ΦR). A solution is not the mere control of (S), but the reopening, reconnection, and regeneration of (ΦR). The evaluative criterion is (d(ΦR)/dt ≥ 0), asking whether generative resonance is sustained or increased over time. The paper applies this framework to climate change, declining birthrates, war, food insecurity, inequality, discrimination, and AI ethics. It further argues that AI intensifies nominal problem-solving by accelerating classification, scoring, prediction, optimization, governance, and compliance, thereby risking the automation of Hyper-S. The paper concludes by redefining philosophy as differential phase diagnosis: the task of reading where problems become named, where names become structures, where structures become closures, and where they may reopen into renewed generative possibility. Highlights The paper introduces nominal problem-solving as a core mechanism by which modern civilization reproduces global problems while attempting to solve them. It argues that global crises are not merely failures of knowledge, technology, funding, or governance, but symptoms of an implicit ontology: (E = S). It develops a UPCT-based alternative in which problems are understood as closures, ruptures, or over-crystallizations of (ΦR). It proposes (d(ΦR)/dt ≥ 0) as a differential criterion for evaluating whether policies, institutions, technologies, and ethical systems sustain generative resonance over time. It shows how AI may accelerate Hyper-S by transforming persons, values, risks, ethics, and institutions into processable structures. It redefines philosophy as phase diagnosis rather than concept definition: philosophy must read where names open reality and where they become closures. It offers a civilizational shift from control to participation, from managing (S) to reopening (ΦR). Contribution to Civilizational Theory This paper contributes to civilizational theory by identifying a shared ontological structure underlying apparently separate global crises. Climate change, demographic decline, war, food insecurity, inequality, discrimination, and AI ethics are usually treated as distinct policy domains. This paper argues that they are connected by a common mode of modern problem-solving: the conversion of dynamic relational crises into nominally manageable (S)-objects. The civilizational contribution lies in showing that modernity does not merely fail because it lacks sufficient solutions, but because its very form of solution often reproduces the logic of the problem. By applying (S) to (S), modern civilization produces increasingly elaborate systems of governance, audit, metrics, regulation, and optimization, while the living fields of ecological, social, familial, cultural, and ethical resonance continue to weaken. UPCT reframes civilization not as a system for controlling problems, but as a field for sustaining generative resonance. A generative-resonant civilization is one that evaluates institutions, policies, economies, technologies, and cultural forms by whether they reopen (ΦR) over time. This offers a civilizational alternative to the modern paradigm of control, optimization, and structural expansion. Philosophical Contribution The paper contributes to philosophy by extending process, relational, and systems-oriented thought into a new diagnostic framework. Rather than asking only what a problem is, the paper asks how a problem becomes named, crystallized, institutionalized, managed, and over-crystallized. This shifts philosophy from nominal definition to differential phase diagnosis. The philosophical innovation lies in the contrast between (E = S) and (E = ΦR). The former names the implicit ontology of modern problem-solving, in which existence becomes structure, object, classification, or measurable form. The latter proposes existence as generative possibility through relational resonance. This allows the paper to reinterpret global crises not as isolated objects, but as phase conditions of blocked or ruptured (ΦR). The criterion (d(ΦR)/dt ≥ 0 ) further transforms philosophical evaluation. Ethics, politics, technology, governance, and social reform are judged not merely by internal consistency, compliance, utility, or institutional success, but by whether they sustain or increase generative resonance over time. Philosophy thus becomes a practice of reading openings and closures in the movement of life. Social Contribution The paper offers a socially useful framework for diagnosing why well-intentioned reforms often generate new problems. Climate policies may reduce emissions while damaging ecological relations. Demographic policies may support childbirth while failing to restore family, love, and future trust. Anti-discrimination policies may protect people while reinforcing categorical perception. AI ethics may expand governance while turning ethics into compliance. By distinguishing between managing (S) and reopening (ΦR), the paper provides a practical lens for evaluating policies, institutions, technologies, and reforms. It does not reject metrics, laws, categories, or governance. Instead, it asks whether these structures remain provisional supports for living processes or become self-reproducing systems detached from human and ecological resonance. Socially, this framework encourages reforms that move beyond target achievement and toward relational regeneration. It asks whether communities become more capable of care, whether people gain pathways of participation, whether institutions support rather than replace judgment, whether technologies deepen rather than flatten relation, and whether society becomes more livable over time. Transformation of Values The value transformation proposed by this paper is a shift from control to participation. Modern civilization often values what can be named, measured, governed, optimized, and controlled. Its dominant question is: how can the problem be managed? UPCT asks a deeper question: does this intervention reopen generative resonance? This entails a shift from noun-centered values to process-centered values. Climate policy must move from carbon management alone to renewed Earth-relation. Demographic policy must move from fertility-rate management to the reopening of love, family, care, time, and future trust. Anti-discrimination must move from attribute management to the restoration of encounter. AI ethics must move from compliance to the question of whether intelligence serves human, social, ecological, and cultural (ΦR). The proposed value shift can be summarized as follows: From control to participation.From optimization to resonance.From compliance to judgment.From classification to encounter.From extraction to regeneration.From target achievement to field renewal.From managing (S) to reopening (ΦR).From solving the noun to healing the process. The paper does not argue that nouns, institutions, numbers, or policies should be abandoned. Rather, it argues that they must be returned to movement. A name should open reality, not close it. A policy should regenerate relation, not merely manage a target. A civilization should not seek merely to control the world, but to participate in its generative becoming. records.title: The Impact of Double Reduction Policy on the China’s Education System
records.venue: Journal of Education Humanities and Social Sciences
records.abstract: On July 24, 2021, the General Offices of the CPC Central Committee and The State Council issued the Opinions on Further Reducing the burden of homework and off-campus training for Students in compulsory Education (referred to as the "double reduction" policy). This policy has since dramatically changed the landscape of shadow education in China and has impacted millions of people, including those in the education industry. Chinese shadow education has been decimated and has taken a significant negative hit, requiring rapid transformation and upgrading to meet the challenge. While this policy has had a positive impact, which resulting in a significant reduction in stress for elementary and middle school students in the K-12 education system, however, the need for abundant educational resources for students has still not been effectively addressed. And this situation will continue to intensify as China's fertility rate continues to decline. This paper describes the description and impact analysis of the policy and uses the education reform in Japan as a research precedent to provide possible effect prediction and improvement options for the double reduction policy.

records.title: Sperm Quality: Past, Present and the Future Knowledge We Need
records.abstract: The assessment of semen quality is used to identify factors thatinfluence sperm performance and diagnose male infertility. From the earliest works to the present day, a considerable number of analytical techniques have been developed. These tests study many aspects of the morphology and physiology of the spermatozoan; however, their ability to predict male fertility remains low. Some of these techniques have been automated, which can make the test results more objective, but others still require subjective evaluation. The introduction of computer-assisted sperm analysis (CASA) systems and flow cytometry has revolutionized sperm quality analysis in recent decades. However, the use of these advanced techniques remains experimental, with only a few of them having successfully led to practical applications in routine commercial semen evaluation. Future sperm biology research should focus on developing analytical techniques that have a greater capacity to predict male fertility and can be used in both the laboratory and the field. Field adaptation will require progress in automation and simplification, to produce precise, economical and efficient techniques. Nevertheless, as technology advances in these analytical tests and research continues, our greater understanding of male fertility will aid the development of new methods of sperm evaluation.

records.title: Evidence to the House of Lords Select Committee on Economic Affairs on Aspects of the Economics of Climate Change
records.abstract: Dependence of damage estimates upon assumptions of economic growth and technological development Greater economic growth could, by increasing emissions, lead to greater damages from climate change. On the other hand, by increasing wealth and advancing technological development and human capital, economic growth would also increase a society's adaptive capacity and reduce those damages. Although analyses of the impacts (or damages) of climate change generally incorporate economic growth into the emissions and climate change scenarios that they use as inputs, these analyses do not adequately account for the increase in adaptive capacity resulting from that very growth. Because of this inconsistency, these analyses generally tend to overstate impacts. For instance, the average GDP per capita for developing countries in 2100 is projected to be $11,000 (in 1990 US$, at market exchange rates) under A2, the slowest economic growth scenario, and $66,500 under A1, the scenario with both the greatest economic growth and largest climate change. By comparison, in 1990 the GDP per capita for Greece, for example, was $8,300 while Switzerland, the country with the highest income level at that time, had a GDP per capita of $34,000. Based on historical experience, one should expect that at the high levels of GDP per capita projected by the IPCC scenarios in 2100, wealth-driven increases in adaptive capacity alone should virtually eliminate damages from many climate-sensitive hazards, e.g., malaria and hunger, whether or not these damages are caused by climate change. Current damage estimates are inflated further because they usually do not adequately account for secular (time-dependent) improvements in technology that, if history is any guide, ought to occur in the future unrelated to economic development. A compelling argument for reducing greenhouse gases is that it would help developing countries cope with climate change. It is asserted that they need this help because their adaptive capacity is weak. Although often true today, this assertion becomes increasingly invalid in the future if developing countries become wealthier and more technologically advanced, per the IPCC's scenarios. Damage assessments frequently overlook this. Are scenario storylines internally consistent in light of historical experience? Regardless of whether the economic growth assumptions used in the IPCC scenarios are justified, their specifications regarding the relationship between wealth and technological ability are, in general, inconsistent with the lessons of economic history. They assume that the less wealthy societies depicted by the B1 and B2 scenarios would have greater environmental protection and employ cleaner and more efficient technologies than the wealthier society characterized by the A1F1 scenario. This contradicts general experience in the real world, where richer countries usually have cleaner technologies. Under the IPCC scenarios, the richer A1 world has the same population as the poorer B1 world, but in fact total fertility rates — a key determinant of population growth rates — are, by and large, lower for richer nations and, over time, have dropped for any given level of GDP per capita (Goklany 2001a). Merits of reallocating expenditures from mitigation to international development Halting climate change at its 1990 level would annually cost substantially more than the $165 billion estimated for the minimally-effective Kyoto Protocol. According to DEFRA-sponsored studies, in 2085, which is at the limit of the foreseeable future, such a halt would reduce the total global population at risk (PAR) due to both climate change and non-climate-change-related causes by 3 percent for malaria, 21 percent for hunger, and 86 percent for coastal flooding, although the total PAR for water shortage might well increase. The benefits associated with halting climate change — and more — can be obtained more economically through “focused adaptation”, i.e., activities focused on reducing vulnerabilities to the above noted climate-sensitive hazards, or through broadly advancing sustainable development in developing countries by meeting the Millennium Development Goals (MDGs) by 2015. In fact, such efforts, which together could annually cost donor countries $150 billion according to UN Millennium Project and World Health Organization studies, should reduce global malaria, hunger, poverty, and lack of access to safe water and sanitation by 50 percent (each); reduce child and maternal mortality by at least 66 percent; provide universal primary education; and reverse growth in AIDS/HIV, and other major diseases. These numbers also indicate that no matter how important climate change might be in this century, for the next several decades it would be far more beneficial for human well-being, especially in developing countries, to deal with non-climate change related factors. Not only would either focused adaptation or adherence to the MDGs provide greater benefits at lesser costs through the foreseeable future than would any emission reduction scheme, they would help solve today's urgent problems sooner and more certainly. Equally important, they would also increase the ability to deal with tomorrow's problems, whether they are caused by climate change or other factors. None of these claims can be reasonably made on behalf of any mitigation scheme today. Accordingly, over the next few decades the focus of climate policy should be to: (a) broadly advance sustainable development, particularly in developing countries since that would generally enhance their adaptive capacity to cope with the many urgent problems they currently face, including many that are climate-sensitive, (b) specifically reduce vulnerabilities to climate-sensitive problems that are urgent today and might be exacerbated by future climate change, and (c) implement “no-regret” emission reduction measures, while (d) concurrently striving to expand the universe of no-regret options through research and development to increase the variety and cost-effectiveness of available mitigation options. Ancillary benefits associated with greenhouse gas (GHG) reductions Some GHG emission control options might provide substantial co-benefits by concurrently reducing problems not directly caused by climate change (e.g., air pollution or lack of sustained economic growth, especially in developing countries). However, in both these instances, the same, or greater, level of co-benefits can be obtained more economically by directly attacking the specific (non-climate change related) problems rather than indirectly through greenhouse gas control. On the other hand, a direct assault on the numerous climate-sensitive hurdles to sustainable development (e.g., hunger, malaria, and many natural disasters) would, as indicated, provide greater benefits more cost-effectively than would efforts to mitigate climate change.

records.title: Does coresidence with grandparents alleviate the negative effect of family size on reading test scores
records.abstract: This paper postulates that co-residence with grandparents may provide children with additional resources in the form of available time, attention, social ties, social control that may be beneficial for children’s school outcomes as a protection against resource dilution. I hypothesize that co-residence with grandparents may offset or at least alleviate the negative effect of larger family on school outcomes. A comparative analysis on 2000 PISA shows that coresidence may be a buffer at lower levels of socieconomic development, but certainly is not in the most advanced societies, where coresidence has both a negative main effect and a negative interaction with family size.

records.title: From high school to the high chair: Education and fertility timing
records.abstract: This paper examines the effect of education on the timing of fertility. First, we use an institutional rule that led to women obtaining qualifications due to their month of birth (Easter Leaving Rule). Second, we exploit a large expansion of post-compulsory schooling that occurred from the late 1980s to the early 1990s. This expansion resulted in the proportion of 18 year olds in full time education rising from around 17% in 1985 to over 35% in the late 1990s. We find that neither the exogenous increase in qualifications as a result of the Easter Leaving Rule nor the expansion in post-compulsory schooling led to a reduction in the probability of having a child as a teenager. However, we do find that both sources of variation in education led to delays in having a child. There is no evidence that the mechanism driving these findings are due to an incapacitation effect. Instead the results point to both a direct human capital effect and an improvement in labour market opportunities as a result of holding qualifications.

records.title: Is climatic regionalization in frame of estimated pedologic-ecological system actual in 21st century?
records.abstract: Abstract Climatic variables defining climatic regions of estimated pedologic-ecological system (EPEU) were calculated based on fifty-year climatic data from 1961 to 2010. Obtained results were subsequently compared to intervals determining individual climatic regions defined by previous climatic data (1901-1950). In many agricultural intense areas sum of air temperature and mean air temperature exceeded upper limit. In terms of precipitation it is especially noticeable in the wet (higher) altitudes. Significant volatility was found for probability of dry periods from April to September. The values of the moisture certainty from April to September for the period 1961-2010 reached to several tens. In the final analysis, the only safe prediction is that the present and future are likely to be very different from the past. It is necessary to take it into account for actualization of EPEU methodology. Among the strongest arguments justifying the need of this actualization is in particular climate development since 1901, technological progress and improved measurement technology as well as automation and development of climate models coupled with simulations of complex characteristics and estimates of future climate. It is evident that the development of climate and other factors have an enormous impact on soil fertility. This should be also taken into consideration when fixing the official price. It is necessary to consider the possible replacement of the existing characteristics by more suitable (for example soil moisture balance). The findings might be summarized in few words: old climatic regions do not reflect actual climatic conditions.

Livelihood Changes of Char (Dry Land) Women Due to Involvement in Activities of the Char Livelihood Program
records.venue: Asian Journal of Agricultural Extension Economics & Sociology
records.abstract: Climatic hazards are common in Bangladesh on delta and riverine island communities, which are large sandbars formed in riverbeds due to silt and alluvium deposition. Specifically, these hazards are caused by the dynamic erosion and accretion of riverbanks. The natural disaster caused by the subsequent sediment buildup on the riverbed and river bank erosion poses a serious threat to the way of life for the residents of Char, particularly the women, by causing damage to or destruction of houses, crops, and family income. The Char Livelihood Program (CLP) attempted to strengthen women's resilience and sense of empowerment while simultaneously improving their livelihoods, nutrition, access to clean water, sanitation, and hygiene habits of char women. This study was mainly undertaken to investigate the extent of changes in the livelihood status of char women due to the involvement in Char Livelihood Program (CLP), explore the factors that may influence the livelihood changes of the char women due to involvement in the CLP. Besides, the problems faced by the char women while working in CLP were also investigated. Data were collected from four villages of Islampur Upazila (sub-district) under Jamalpur district purposively and analyzed using Multiple Linear Regression Models. The goal was to identify the variables that affect the char women's changes in their livelihood. Findings indicated that involvement in char livelihood program had significant influence on the livelihood of char women. The main factor included years of schooling, family size and knowledge of CLP. Collectively, the factors explained 32.3% variation in the livelihood changes of char women. The most influential challenges, from highest to lowest, included unavailability of transport and poor communication status, and lack of commitment of the service provider. Therefore, in order to overcome these obstacles, efforts must be made to ensure seasonal transportation system and enhance road communication infrastructure to enable char women to move around freely in order to carry agricultural products and to connect with relevant stakeholders for better farming and income operations.

records.title: ALT pedometer - a new sensor-aided measurement system for improvement in oestrus detection
records.abstract: Without sensor-aided animal data measuring systems far fewer oestrus cycles are recognized because cycle length, oestrus duration and oestrus intensity have developed negatively at high animal performance rates. This development makes it eminently clear that observation of the mating season in the dairy cattle sector is even more important than assumed so far if the financial losses due to insufficient herd fertility are not to become a business problem. Electronic identification and measuring systems represent key technologies for progressive automation in animal husbandry in modern, future-oriented livestock farming. Suitable objective measuring systems are needed in animals husbandry to quickly and safely recognize animal illness, normal oestrus cycle, silent heat or suffering from stress. Pedometer and transponder from different companies play an important role for measuring from animals data and statements in animals health and oestrus monitoring. Modern sensors (sensors, bio sensors), increasingly non-invasive measuring and transfer methods make crucial improvements in the potential for measuring animal data. A new type of pedometer, called ALT pedometer, for three measurement parameters (activity, lying time, temperature), a real time watch and a change measuring time interval was developed. With this system it is possible to select different time intervals between 1 and 60 min for continuous measuring. The results for oestrus detection are excellent. The high correspondence between the measuring parameters activity and lying time allow a statement to be made early and safely on animal illnesses and the time of the oestrus cycle.

How Population Aging Drives Labor Productivity: Evidence from China
records.abstract: Population aging is a critical demographic trend in China, presenting both challenges and opportunities for advancing sustainable development in alignment with the UN’s SDGs, particularly SDG 8, Decent Work and Economic Growth, SDG 9,Industry, Innovation, and Infrastructure,SDG 10,Reduced Inequalities. This study investigates the impact of population aging on labor productivity, with a focus on the mediating role of the capital-labor ratio and heterogeneities across industries, skill levels, and regions. Using data from Chinese listed firms between 2011 and 2018,this paper used fixed effects models and mediation models for econometric regressions to explore the relationship between population aging and labor productivity. The analysis reveals that population aging significantly enhances labor productivity. The capital-labor ratio emerges as a critical mechanism, mediating the relationship between aging and productivity by incentivizing firms to increase capital intensity in response to labor shortages. The findings highlight notable heterogeneities. Labor-intensive firms and low-skilled worker segments experience stronger productivity gains from aging compared to their capital-intensive and high-skilled counterparts. At the regional level, the productivity effects are most pronounced in first- and second-tier cities, while third-tier cities show negligible impacts, reflecting resource and structural constraints. This study underscores the dual role of population aging as a challenge and an opportunity. Policy recommendations include promoting capital investment, automation, workforce upskilling, and regional development to sustain productivity growth amidst demographic transitions. These findings offer valuable insights for policymakers and businesses navigating the complexities of aging economies.

records.title: A Survey of Agriculture Applications Utilizing Raspberry Pi
records.abstract: Raspberry Pi is one of the most popular electronic prototyping boards used for prototyping the applications such as Home, Industry, Research, Agriculture etc. This paper provides a summary of Raspberry Pi adoption in agriculture to aid researchers in their work for remote sensing, controlling and automation. Soil quality testing, crop selection, soil fertility and productivity detection, weather monitoring, crop yield detection, plant growth monitoring and automatic spraying of fertilizers and pesticides are some of the Raspberry Pi applications which range from simple solutions to dedicated custom-built devices. The focus was mainly on different farming applications in which information is collected and processed to provide advice to farmers to make right decisions in right time with optimal expenditure. Research challenges, limitations and future trends associated with automated application development using Raspberry Pi are also presented.
